content: Lactucarium is a milky fluid secreted by various species of lettuce, most notably Lactuca virosa. This fluid is typically excreted from the base of the plant's stems. It is often referred to as lettuce opium due to its sedative and analgesic properties. Lactucarium has been reported to induce a mild sensation of euphoria. However, Lactuca virosa is toxic, and at least one fatality has been documented in an attempt to use it for intoxication purposes. As a latex, lactucarium physically resembles opium, as it is secreted as a white fluid that can be processed into a thick, solid form that is smokable. Historically, lettuce opium was utilized by the Ancient Egyptians and was introduced as a drug in the United States as early as 1799. During the 19th century, it was extensively studied and prescribed in Poland as a weaker alternative to opium, with the advantage of lacking significant side effects. In some cases, it was even considered preferable to opium. However, early attempts to isolate an active alkaloid from lactucarium were unsuccessful. It was described and standardized in the 1898 United States Pharmacopeia and the 1911 British Pharmaceutical Codex for use in lozenges, tinctures, and syrups. These preparations were intended as sedatives for irritable coughs or as mild hypnotics to aid with insomnia. The official definition of lactucarium in these codices required its production from Lactuca virosa, though it was acknowledged that smaller quantities could be derived from Lactuca sativa, Lactuca canadensis var. elongata, and even Lactuca scariola or Lactuca altissima, the latter of which was considered to yield a superior product. In the 20th century, two major studies found that commercial lactucarium lacked any significant effects. In 1944, Fulton concluded that modern medicine considers its sleep-producing qualities a superstition, its therapeutic action doubtful or nil. Another study from the same period identified active bitter principles, lactucin and lactucopicrin, but noted that these compounds were unstable in fresh latex and did not persist in commercial preparations of lactucarium. Consequently, the use of lettuce opium fell out of favor until the 1970s, when publications associated with the hippie movement began promoting it as a legal drug capable of producing euphoria. It was sometimes compounded with other herbs such as catnip or damiana. Additionally, lettuce seeds were historically used for pain relief until the 17th century. In contemporary times, lactucarium has largely faded from general use as a pain reliever but remains available in some contexts, occasionally marketed as a legal psychotropic substance. The seeds of common lettuce (Lactuca sativa) are still used in traditional medicine in regions such as Iran, where a crude extract of the seeds has been shown to exhibit analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects in laboratory rats during formalin and carrageenan tests. This extract was found to be non-toxic to rats at doses of up to 6 grams per kilogram. The active components of lactucarium are believed to include lactucin and its derivatives, lactucopicrin and 11β,13-dihydrolactucin. These compounds have demonstrated analgesic activity comparable to or greater than that of ibuprofen in standard pain sensitivity tests, such as the hot-plate and tail-flick tests in laboratory mice. Additionally, lactucin and lactucopicrin have been shown to possess sedative properties, as evidenced by reductions in spontaneous movements in mice. Some effects of lactucarium have also been attributed to trace amounts of hyoscyamine in Lactuca virosa, though this alkaloid was undetectable in standard lactucarium preparations.
